rows.source: Sea-web Output Statistics and Internal Arithmetic: Provincial Yards 1,168 Ships / 5.1 Million dwt (10.7%), NACKS 3.7 Million dwt (7.7%), Domestic Buyers 13 Million dwt (27.1%), Regional Shares (36.7 + 23.9 + 21.8) and the Seafarer Census (pp. 12, 15–16, 18, 20, 38–39, Notes 31, 33, 104)
rows.usage: Builds the picture of a coastal, export-oriented industry from Lloyd's Register-Fairplay Sea-web tallies since the 1999 CSSC/CSIC split, and measures China's seafaring labor pool against the United States.
rows.finding: Verified by internal cross-check (`ok`): the three percentage-of-total claims imply the same PRC total (5.1 ÷ 0.107 ≈ 47.7, 3.7 ÷ 0.077 ≈ 48.1 and 13 ÷ 0.271 ≈ 48.0 million dwt); provincial output of 5.1 million dwt is 2.6 times the 1.94 million dwt of 1982–99 (Note 31), consistent with 'more than double'; 36.7 + 23.9 + 21.8 = 82.4%, consistent with 'over 80 percent'; 26 CSSC/CSIC yards at 12% of yards implies about 216 new-construction yards; and the seafarer percentages (122,208 = 9.96%; 20,560 = 1.68%) imply the same world total of about 1.22–1.23 million. The Sea-web figures themselves are a proprietary database and could not be re-pulled.

rows.source: Shipyard Productivity Gap: $9,000 per Worker vs. $550,000 (Japan) and $480,000 (Korea), 'One-Sixth' Productivity and Workforce Counts of 275,000 / 72,000 / 40,000 (pp. 2, 37, Notes 97–99)
rows.usage: Cites a Chinese analyst (Zhang Kai, 2006) for per-worker output and a European Metalworkers' Federation report for workforce sizes, to argue that productivity and management weaknesses will hinder naval shipbuilding as well.
rows.finding: Quoted faithfully, but the headline ratio does not reconcile (`unk`): the Executive Summary calls $9,000 'an order of magnitude lower' than $550,000/$480,000 (the actual ratios are about 61× and 53×), and p. 37 simultaneously says productivity is 'roughly one-sixth' of Japan's or Korea's. Multiplying the cited per-worker figures by the cited workforces gives roughly $2.5 billion for China (275,000 × $9,000), $40 billion for Japan (72,000 × $550,000) and $19 billion for Korea (40,000 × $480,000) — implying Japan builds twice as much as Korea and sixteen times as much as China, which contradicts the paper's own near-equal Japan/Korea tonnage shares (32–35% each) and China's 13.8–20%. The inputs are Chinese-analyst and NGO estimates that could not be traced to a primary dataset. Follow-up review, November 15, 2026. Using the table’s stated inputs, the Japanese and Korean figures are about 61 and 53 times China’s, respectively. The table therefore cannot support the separate one-sixth characterization on the same basis. The workforce definitions and underlying output figures still need to be matched before generalizing.

paper_memo.memo_title: Analytical & Source-Audit Memo: CMS-01 — A Comprehensive Survey of China's Dynamic Shipbuilding Industry (Gabriel Collins & Lt. Cdr. Michael C. Grubb, CMSI, 2008)

sections.heading: 1. Strategic Context & Core Thesis
sections.body: China Maritime Study No. 1 launched the CMSI Red Book series in August 2008 with a **comprehensive survey of China's shipbuilding industry**. Written by Gabriel Collins (energy and shipbuilding fellow) and Lt. Cdr. Michael Grubb (a submarine officer and naval architect writing as a student), it asks how much China's commercial shipbuilding boom matters for the PLA Navy. The authors' bottom line is carefully hedged: China's drive 'is not at present primarily driven by military factors but rather by commercial incentives,' yet it is 'adding very extensive latent maritime capacity that Beijing could draw upon in a future maritime rivalry or conflict' (p. 4). Their method is to combine Lloyd's Sea-web registry data on every Chinese new-construction yard since the 1999 CSSC/CSIC split with Chinese trade-press sources, shipowner interviews and a visit to the November 2007 MARINTEC exhibition in Shanghai.

sections.heading: 2. Section-by-Section Analytical Breakdown
sections.body:
• **Executive Summary & Introduction (pp. 1–5)**: Sets out the CNO's concern, the 49% foreign-ownership cap, the 2015 world-number-one goal and the 'strategic reserve' of shipbuilders.
• **Historical Evolution (pp. 5–8)**: Six reasons shipbuilding converted to commercial work more successfully than aerospace: early corporatization (1982 vs. AVIC's 1993), low technological hurdles, early foreign contact, balanced domestic and export demand, coastal geography and cheap labor.
• **The Industry Today (pp. 9–22)**: CSSC/CSIC rivalry, public listings (Hudong Heavy Machinery's 400 million shares, over 12 billion RMB), joint-venture and private yards, PLA Navy Factories 4807/4808, regional concentration (Shanghai 36.7%, Liaoning 23.9%, Jiangsu 21.8%) and the shift to VLCCs, containerships and LNG carriers.
• **Commercial–Military Synergies (pp. 22–39)**: Five technology areas — production methods, systems integration, hull metallurgy, subcomponents and propulsion — plus 'human factors.'
• **Conclusions (pp. 39–45)**: Market prospects, a thought experiment in which one greenfield yard turns to warships, and the four indicators to watch.

sections.heading: 3. Key Doctrinal Concepts, Terminology & Quantitative Claims
sections.body:
• **Concepts**: *Hull-block construction* (modular assembly, 'grand blocks'), *greenfield yards* (Waigaoqiao, Changxing Island, Longxue, Dalian No. 2, Haixiwan), *defense conversion* ('from swords to plowshares . . . and better swords,' quoting Folta), *CHISREP* (China Ship Reporting System), *brand-name suppliers* and market-access-for-technology deals in marine equipment.
• **Quantitative claims**: `13.8%` of world gross tonnage in 2005; `29.6` million CGT of 2007 orders vs. Korea's `32` million; `24` million tons / `35%` of capacity targeted for 2015; `30` VLCC docks by 2015 (9 by 2008); `1,168` provincial ships / `5.1` million dwt; `40%` indigenous subcomponents (60% by 2010, 80% by 2015); `53` commercial and `72` PLAN ships with SEMT-Pielstick diesels; Chinese-designed engines `11%` of medium-speed and `<1%` of low-speed plants; `303` yards suspended and `586` ships failed in the 2005 quality campaign; `$9,000` vs. `$550,000` per-worker output.

sections.heading: 4. Audit Assessment & Analytical Significance
sections.body:
Of the 6 reference rows audited in `CMS-01`, 3 are rated `ok` (one with a minor counting slip), 2 are `unk` and **1 is rated `fix` (`[CMS01-R04]`)**:
• **`[CMS01-R04]` (`fix` — First Chinese-Built LNG Carrier Delivered in 'Early 2007')**: The paper dates the first Chinese LNG tanker delivery to 2007 on the strength of a February 2007 forecast; *Dapeng Sun* was delivered in April 2008.
• **`[CMS01-R03]` (`unk` — Productivity Gap)**: The 'order of magnitude' and 'one-sixth' framings are mutually inconsistent, and the per-worker and workforce figures cannot be reconciled with the paper's own tonnage shares; the claim is quoted faithfully but should be treated as an unreliable estimate.
• **`[CMS01-R02]` (`ok` — Internal Arithmetic)**: The percentage-of-total claims, regional shares and seafarer census all cross-check, which supports the Sea-web tallies even though the database itself could not be re-pulled.

As a baseline, this study is valuable less for its forecasts (China hit its 2015 target years early and CSSC and CSIC were re-merged in 2019) than for its **indicator framework**: Jiangnan's 2009 move to Changxing Island and the later carrier and destroyer output there show the indicators were well chosen, even though the answer proved to be 'both.'

**Footnote rows**: all 111 footnotes were extracted and consolidated into 91 source rows in the Reference Audit Matrix (CMS01-N001 to CMS01-N112). Repeat citations of the same source within this paper, including Ibid. and short-form notes, share one row, which lists each note's passage and result. Footnote-level result: 111 notes: 22 (20%) are confirmed, 0 of them against a retrieved source and 22 after an outside web search (17 of the latter with a slip or an unchecked detail noted); 7 are flagged for reader check; 89 (80%) are not confirmed. Of the 89 notes not confirmed, 3 are Chinese-language sources that have not been searched in Chinese (a search in Chinese could settle some of them); 20 were judged not web-checkable (13 the authors' own data, imagery or analysis; 3 private interviews or conversations; 2 print-only books or paywalled items; 2 notes that are explanatory text or a fragment, not a citation); 66 were searched on the web without finding corroboration. A source row is `ok` only when every note in it is confirmed, and `fix` when a note is confirmed wrong; the paper's 91 source rows are 17 `ok`, 0 `fix` and 74 `unk`. Notes flagged for reader check, for example (the outside search found something a reader should look at; none is a finding that the author is wrong): `CMS01-N003`: The sentence says Chinese yards account for roughly 20 percent of the global shipbuilding market with an estimated 80 percent of gross output (S1) or of ships built in 2006 (S2) slated for export; `CMS01-N022`: The sentence says CSSC's diesel engine builder Hudong Heavy Machinery recently "went public" with four hundred million shares valued at over twelve billion RMB. Reports describe a placement of up to 400 million new A shares at 30 yuan (for about nine billion yuan of assets and three billion yuan of cash) by an already…; `CMS01-N028`: The sentence gives a target of 24 million deadweight tons, or 35 percent of world shipbuilding, by 2015. Reports of the time give lower targets: about 14–15 million deadweight tons for CSSC and CSIC combined by 2015, and a one-third or 30 percent world share; and 4 more. 26 notes carry a reader note on how the note is displayed or cited.

paper_memo.memo_title: Analytical & Source-Audit Memo: CANP-00 — Introduction, China's Assertive Nuclear Posture (Baohui Zhang, 2015)

sections.heading: 1. Strategic Context & Core Thesis
sections.body: In the Introduction to *China's Assertive Nuclear Posture*, Baohui Zhang (Lingnan University) argues that scholars of Chinese nuclear policy have a **'status quo bias'**: because they emphasize unit-level constraints (strategic culture, Mao's and Deng's ideas, technology, bureaucratic politics), they miss rapid change. A **structural-realist** lens — anarchy, balancing, the security dilemma and the end of unipolarity — explains two simultaneous shifts: a build-up of offensive forces plus space and missile-defense programs aimed at US missile defense, and a 'tacit modification' of no-first-use during the 2012 East China Sea crisis with Japan. The chapter's job is to frame the evidence (four 2012 missile tests, a 2013 submarine publicity push, the 2013 white-paper omission of NFU) and preview the book's chapters.

sections.heading: 2. Section-by-Section Analytical Breakdown
sections.body:
• **Opening Evidence (pp. 1–3)**: The 2012 test cluster, the October 2013 CCTV/newspaper submarine publicity and the white-paper omission are presented as a pattern of 'nuclear signaling.'
• **Structural Realism and China's Nuclear Posture (pp. 3–5)**: Waltz's survival assumption, Walt's balance of threat (judged a 'trivial' dichotomy), defensive realism's security dilemma and offensive realism's power maximization.
• **Major Contributions (pp. 5–6)**: Dynamic explanation, theory-building from the Chinese case, crisis-behavior evidence and a reading of the 2013 SMS.
• **Plan of the Book (pp. 6–11)**: Previews of Chapters 1–6 and the Conclusion, including the 300–400 warhead projection, the integrated nuclear-space strategy and the possibility of a Japanese nuclear response.
• **Endnotes (pp. 11–12)**: Ten notes; the Chinese-language material is mostly Sohu/government web sources.

sections.heading: 3. Key Doctrinal Concepts, Terminology & Quantitative Claims
sections.body:
• **Concepts**: *minimum deterrence*, *no-first-use* (NFU), *tacit modification*, *balance of power vs. balance of threat*, *strategic opportunity period* (said to have begun with the 2001 terrorist attacks on the USA), *three-dimensional posture* (offense plus space warfare plus missile defense), *leaping to parity*.
• **Quantitative claims**: `4` strategic missile tests in `2` months of 2012; DF-41 `up to 10` warheads; `300 to 400` strategic warheads projected (a figure the book restates differently in Chapter 2 [300–500] and Chapter 7 [400–500, then 510–980]); New START `1,550` and a proposed `1,000` warheads.

sections.heading: 4. Audit Assessment & Analytical Significance
sections.body:
Of the 5 reference rows audited in `CANP-00`, 4 are rated `ok` (two with citation slips) and 1 is rated `unk`; none rises to a `fix`:
• **`[CANP00-R02]` (`ok · slip` — White-Paper Title and Date)**: The omission of NFU from the 16 April 2013 white paper is real, but Note 3 mis-dates and mis-translates the document ('April 2014,' 'Diversified Deployment').
• **`[CANP00-R03]` (`unk` — Pentagon 2014 Quotation)**: The quotation and its p. 28 pin cite could not be confirmed.
• **`[CANP00-R01]` (`ok` — 2012 Tests)**: The test sequence is confirmed by contemporaneous reporting, but the 'signaling' reading is inferential.

The Introduction is best read as a **thesis statement**: its warhead projection was overtaken by events and its NFU claim was not adopted as doctrine, which is why the dashboard pairs it with the chapters that carry the evidence (`CANP-C2`, `CANP-C7`) and with the DoD and SIPRI series on the actual arsenal.

**Footnote rows**: all 10 footnotes were extracted and consolidated into 9 source rows in the Reference Audit Matrix (CANP00-N001 to CANP00-N010). paper_memo.memo_title: Analytical & Source-Audit Memo: CANP-C2 — Chapter 2: China's Nuclear Forces and Doctrines (Baohui Zhang, 2015)

sections.heading: 1. Strategic Context & Core Thesis
sections.body: Chapter 2 of Baohui Zhang's *China's Assertive Nuclear Posture* is the book's descriptive backbone. It supplies (1) a history of China's nuclear forces following Peng Guangqian's three phases, (2) an inventory of today's land, sea and air nuclear forces, (3) the two core doctrines — **minimum deterrence** and **no-first-use** — through the writings of PLA strategists Peng Guangqian and Yao Yunzhu, and (4) the tensions that have pushed some Chinese analysts toward *limited deterrence* and a *conditional* NFU. Its original contribution is a close reading of the **2013 edition of the PLA Academy of Military Science's *Science of Military Strategy*** (SMS), which Zhang interprets as assigning nuclear weapons the job of deterring crises and wars in general, thereby conflicting with NFU.

sections.heading: 2. Section-by-Section Analytical Breakdown
sections.body:
• **China's Quest for Nuclear Deterrence (PDF pp. 1–5)**: Balancing motives (Lewis & Xue, Zhu Mingquan, Goldstein), Soviet aid and its collapse, and the 1964 first test.
• **Today's Forces (PDF pp. 5–7)**: DF-3/4/5, DF-31/31A/41, Type 094/JL-2, H-6K and the DF-21/25/26 theater missiles, with Table 2.1.
• **Nuclear Doctrines (PDF pp. 7–10)**: Peng's four principles and Yao's five characteristics; PLA *Strategic Deterrence* (Ning Ling et al., 2010) on 'several dozen' warheads as sufficient.
• **Tensions within the Doctrines (PDF pp. 11–15)**: Johnston on limited deterrence; You Ji; Zhu Chenghu (2005); Shen Dingli; Peng & Rong; Zhu Mingquan and Wu Tianfu.
• **Strategic Deterrence and the 2013 SMS (PDF pp. 15–21)**: Strategic opportunity period, 'effective control,' crisis management and the role of nuclear deterrence at the core of strategic deterrence.
• **China's Changing Nuclear Posture (PDF pp. 21–23)**: Four changes: expansion beyond minimum deterrence, a three-dimensional posture, an announced tactical capability and a modified NFU.

sections.heading: 3. Key Doctrinal Concepts, Terminology & Quantitative Claims
sections.body:
• **Concepts**: *minimum deterrence* ('small but effective'), *no-first-use*, *limited deterrence*, *conditional NFU*, *strategic opportunity period*, *effective control* of crises, *integrated nuclear-conventional deterrence*, *assured retaliation vs. assured destruction*, *counter-value strategy*.
• **Quantitative claims**: first test `16 Oct 1964`; JL-1 test `12 Oct 1982`; Pentagon 2012 missile table (`50–75` ICBMs, `1,000–1,200` SRBMs); Jin-class `3` delivered, `up to 2` more (DoD 2013); JL-2 range `>7,400 km`; DF-25 `3` warheads / `3,200 km`; DF-26 `4,500 km`; posture of `300–500` strategic warheads; PLA study on `several dozen` warheads; SMS page references `p. 152` and `p. 172`.

sections.heading: 4. Audit Assessment & Analytical Significance
sections.body:
Of the 6 reference rows audited in `CANP-C2`, 3 are rated `ok`, 2 are `unk` and **1 is rated `fix` (`[CANPC2-R02]`)**:
• **`[CANPC2-R02]` (`fix` — Mao's Atomic-Bomb Remark Dated 25 April 1955)**: The quoted speech is Mao's *Ten Major Relationships* talk of **25 April 1956**; the chapter's own timeline (decision in April 1956) contradicts the 1955 date.
• **`[CANPC2-R04]` (`unk` — DF-25 / DF-26 Claims)**: The MIRVed DF-25 and 4,500-km DF-26 come from Chinese web media and were not borne out by later official inventories.
• **`[CANPC2-R06]` (`unk` — SMS 'Genuine Change' Reading)**: The chapter's key interpretive step cannot be checked against the Chinese text, and the SMS passage it concedes (p. 172) points the other way.

The chapter is a **useful digest of Chinese nuclear doctrine literature** (Peng, Yao, Johnston, You Ji) but a weak basis for the book's thesis: the history and doctrine sections audit cleanly, while the claims that carry the argument rely on web-media and interpretive readings that later Chinese official documents did not confirm.

**Footnote rows**: all 109 footnotes were extracted and consolidated into 30 source rows in the Reference Audit Matrix (CANPC2-N001 to CANPC2-N110). Repeat citations of the same source within this paper, including Ibid. and short-form notes, share one row, which lists each note's passage and result. Footnote-level result: 109 notes: 16 (15%) are confirmed, 0 of them against a retrieved source and 16 after an outside web search (13 of the latter with a slip or an unchecked detail noted); 1 is flagged for reader check; 93 (85%) are not confirmed. Of the 93 notes not confirmed, 61 are Chinese-language sources that have not been searched in Chinese (a search in Chinese could settle some of them); 4 were judged not web-checkable (4 print-only books or paywalled items); 27 were searched on the web without finding corroboration; 1 has not been searched. A source row is `ok` only when every note in it is confirmed, and `fix` when a note is confirmed wrong; the paper's 30 source rows are 6 `ok`, 0 `fix` and 24 `unk`. Notes flagged for reader check, for example (the outside search found something a reader should look at; none is a finding that the author is wrong): `CANPC2-N033`: The sentence gives 4,500 km as the DF-26's range. Reports found (2016 coverage, The Diplomat) most often estimate 3,000–4,000 km, with some at 4,000–5,000 km, so 4,500 km sits at the high end of published estimates. 15 notes carry a reader note on how the note is displayed or cited.

paper_memo.memo_title: Analytical & Source-Audit Memo: CANP-C7 — Chapter 7: Conclusion and 'Leaping to Parity' Scenarios (Baohui Zhang, 2015)

sections.heading: 1. Strategic Context & Core Thesis
sections.body: Chapter 7 closes Baohui Zhang's *China's Assertive Nuclear Posture* by claiming vindication for **structural realism**: balancing against American missile defense and the security dilemma explain China's force expansion, while balance-of-threat logic against Japan explains the 'tacit' erosion of no-first-use. Technological and doctrinal explanations are folded in as downstream of structure. Looking ahead, the chapter switches from **defensive** to **offensive realism**, arguing that Xi Jinping's 'China Dream' and the 'new type of major power relations' may drive Beijing to seek **strategic and nuclear parity** with Washington, and it offers two scenarios of 510–650 and 780–980 strategic warheads to show that this is within reach.

sections.heading: 2. Section-by-Section Analytical Breakdown
sections.body:
• **Anarchy, Security, and Structural Primacy (PDF pp. 1–3)**: Missile defense, space warfare and the East China Sea as structural evidence; a rebuttal of liberal institutionalism.
• **Evaluating the Structural Approach (PDF pp. 3–6)**: A comparison with the technological perspective (Roberts) and the doctrinal perspective (Johnston) and an argument that both are driven by structural imperatives.
• **Offensive Realism and China's Nuclear Future (PDF pp. 6–8)**: The China Dream, the Soviet analogy, New START and the Obama proposal, and Scenarios 1 and 2 (Tables 7.1 and 7.2).
• **Closing Argument (PDF p. 8)**: PLA Academy of Military Science's *Strategic Assessment 2013* on missile defense and the claim that offensive and defensive realist dynamics together point to parity.

sections.heading: 3. Key Doctrinal Concepts, Terminology & Quantitative Claims
sections.body:
• **Concepts**: *structural primacy*, *assured retaliation vs. assured destruction*, *co-super power*, *new type of major power relations*, *defensive vs. offensive positionalism*, *leaping to parity*, *action-reaction spiral*.
• **Quantitative claims**: `1,550` (New START by 2018) and `1,000` (Obama proposal) warheads; `400–500` warheads (text) vs. `510–650` (Scenario 1) and `780–980` (Scenario 2); `5` or `8` Type 094 SSBNs × `12` JL-2 × `5` warheads (`300` / `480`); `20` / `30` DF-41 × `6–10`; `30` / `40` DF-31A × `3–5`; an SSBN force of `8–12` boats; the claim that Russia and the USA each have `12` SSBNs.

sections.heading: 4. Audit Assessment & Analytical Significance
sections.body:
Of the 5 reference rows audited in `CANP-C7`, 3 are rated `ok` (all with minor slips) and **2 are rated `fix` (`[CANPC7-R02]`, `[CANPC7-R04]`)**:
• **`[CANPC7-R02]` (`fix` — Headline Warhead Forecast vs. Scenario Totals)**: The text says '400 to 500' for a force that Table 7.1 totals at 510–650, and the book gives four different ranges (300–400, 300–500, 400–500, 510–650) for the same capability.
• **`[CANPC7-R04]` (`fix` — 'Both Russia and the USA Maintain 12 SSBNs')**: The United States operated 14 Ohio-class SSBNs; the benchmark behind the affordability claim is wrong.
• **`[CANPC7-R01]` (`ok · slip` — Scenario Tables)**: The arithmetic in Tables 7.1 and 7.2 is correct once the '5x12x5' label for eight boats is read as 8×12×5.

The chapter's value is its **explicit, checkable scenario method** — assumptions are stated and the sums add up — rather than its precision: the headline forecast contradicts its own tables, the warhead-per-missile inputs are the author's assumptions, and later events (a stockpile above 600, silo expansion) outran the scenarios without confirming the parity motive.

**Footnote rows**: all 16 footnotes were extracted and added to the Reference Audit Matrix as source rows (CANPC7-N001 to CANPC7-N016), each with its citing sentence and the result of the check. Footnote-level result: 16 notes: 8 (50%) are confirmed, 0 of them against a retrieved source and 8 after an outside web search (7 of the latter with a slip or an unchecked detail noted); 1 is flagged for reader check; 8 (50%) are not confirmed. Of the 8 notes not confirmed, 8 were searched on the web without finding corroboration. A source row is `ok` only when every note in it is confirmed, and `fix` when a note is confirmed wrong; the paper's 16 source rows are 8 `ok`, 0 `fix` and 8 `unk`. Notes flagged for reader check, for example (the outside search found something a reader should look at; none is a finding that the author is wrong): `CANPC7-N006`: The note gives the title as 'China and Ballistic Missile Defense: 1955 to 2020 and Beyond'; the OSTI, DTIC and IFRI listings found give '1955 to 2002 and Beyond' (IDA Paper P-3826, September 2003). 2 notes carry a reader note on how the note is displayed or cited.

**Open-claim evidence follow-up, November 22, 2026 — Reviewed; unresolved.** The supplied chapter's opening page explicitly contrasts a centrally controlled Soviet system with a Chinese system combining centrally directed and entrepreneurial acquisition, including both open and clandestine routes. The earlier shorthand that the chapter presents acquisition as mostly secret overstates that wording. The 1980 sample count is a separate historical claim, and the extract's opening assertion cannot itself verify it. The argument against a grains-of-sand model is an interpretation of a selected case record, not a measured population estimate. This continuation does not recover the Soviet acquisition tally or establish how representative prosecuted cases are of all acquisition.

**Remaining gap or scope limit.** Original Soviet acquisition tally and an explicit sampling frame for generalizing from the prosecuted case record.

**Earlier audit record (preserved).** Argument not independently testable (`unk`): the Soviet comparison ('thousands' of items, 'particularly notable success in 1980') rests on Note 1, whose text is not in the excerpt, and the claim that the case record 'does not point to' a grains-of-sand approach is an inference from a catalog of prosecuted cases, which by construction over-represents publicly charged defendants. The Made in China 2025 reference is accurate, though the program was later publicly de-emphasized.

paper_memo.memo_title: Analytical & Source-Audit Memo: CCE-C4 — Chapter 4: Economic Espionage Cases (Peter Mattis & Matthew Brazil, 2019)

sections.heading: 1. Strategic Context & Core Thesis
sections.body: Chapter 4 of *Chinese Communist Espionage: An Intelligence Primer* is the book's **catalog of economic-espionage cases**. In a short introduction, Peter Mattis and Matthew Brazil argue that China's technology acquisition is a **hybrid** system — centrally directed by Five-Year Plan and Made in China 2025 goals, run partly by intelligence officers, partly by state-owned enterprises and partly by independent students and entrepreneurs — and that the evidence 'does not point to a grains of sand approach.' About 120 alphabetical entries (agricultural seeds, defense electronics, aerospace, nuclear engineering, chemicals, wind turbines and cyber intrusions) supply the evidence, with cross-references to Chapter 6's case on Chi Mak.

sections.heading: 2. Section-by-Section Analytical Breakdown
sections.body:
• **Framing Essay (PDF p. 1)**: Directorate T / Line X comparison, Five-Year Plans and Made in China 2025, and the 'grains of sand' rebuttal.
• **Corporate and Agricultural Cases (PDF pp. 1–19)**: Dabeinong / Kings Nower Seed, Liew / Pangang / DuPont, Dow, Motorola, GM, Pittsburgh Corning, Cargill, CGNPG, Sinovel.
• **Export-Control and Defense Cases (PDF pp. 2–26)**: Thermal imagers, encryption devices, night vision, amplifiers, UAV autopilots, radiation-hardened circuits and military parts.
• **Aerospace and Stealth Cases (PDF pp. 4–6)**: Chung and Gowadia.
• **Cyber and Talent-Program Entries (PDF pp. 6–25)**: Unit 61398 individuals, CETC, SAFEA, SMIC, Datang.

sections.heading: 3. Key Doctrinal Concepts, Terminology & Quantitative Claims
sections.body:
• **Concepts**: *hybrid* technology acquisition, *grains of sand*, state-owned-enterprise operations, Entity List 'presumption of denial,' FISA surveillance of corporate targets, talent-recruitment programs, export-control front companies and false end-user certificates.
• **Case Metrics**: `~120` entries (`112` dated cases plus `8` organization profiles); Liew: `15` years, `$27.8` million forfeited, `$511,667.82` restitution; Chung: `188` months; Gowadia: `32` years; Sinovel / AMSC: `~$800 million` claimed losses and a `$1.7 million` six-year contract offer to Karabasevic; Dabeinong: `1.08%` state-fund stake, `18,000` employees, `67` subsidiaries; CETC: `150,000` employees and three Entity-List institutes; DuPont-linked profits `$27.8 million`.

sections.heading: 4. Audit Assessment & Analytical Significance
sections.body:
Of the 6 reference rows audited in `CCE-C4`, 5 are rated `ok` (three with minor slips) and 1 is rated `unk`; no substantive `fix` was found:
• **`[CCEC4-R01]` (`ok · slip` — 'American Semiconductor' for American Superconductor)**: Two of the three Sinovel entries misname AMSC even though the third gets it right.
• **`[CCEC4-R02]` (`ok · slip` — Liew Restitution Labeled a Fine)**: The convictions and sentence are correct but a restitution order is described as 'fines.'
• **`[CCEC4-R03]` (`ok · slip` — Chung's 188-Month Sentence)**: 'Fifteen years' understates the sentence by eight months.
• **`[CCEC4-R06]` (`unk` — 'Not Grains of Sand')**: The framing is an inference from prosecuted cases and the Soviet comparison could not be verified.

The chapter is a **reliable, case-by-case reference** — every dated outcome we sampled matched Justice Department records — while its larger claim about the character of Chinese technology transfer is a judgment about a sample that prosecutors, not the authors, selected.

The PDF of this book chapter does not include its endnotes, so its notes could not be turned into rows.

rows.source: The 10 November 2004 Han-Class SSN Incident: Submerged Transit of the Ishigaki Strait, Maritime Security Operations Alert (Second Since 1945), Chinese 'Regret' and the Five-Day Diplomatic Silence (pp. 4–5, 16–17, 23, Notes 16–21, 64–68, 83)
rows.usage: Builds the central case study on the Han's incursion, the JMSDF tracking response, the PRC vice foreign minister's statement that the submarine 'accidentally strayed' for a 'technical reason,' and the delay in the PRC response.
rows.finding: Verified in substance (`ok`): Japan's 10–12 November 2004 detection and tracking, the Defense Agency's high-level alert (the first such alert since 1945 was in 1999 over North Korean vessels, as Note 19 states), China's expression of regret to Japan's ambassador, and the APEC-Santiago Hu–Koizumi meeting on 21 November all match Japanese and wire reporting. The 'five-day delay' and the inference that the Foreign Ministry was unaware of the PLAN's action rest on press accounts, and the meeting is 'just days' after only by eleven days.

rows.source: PLAN Submarine Order of Battle: ~38 Boats Commissioned 1995–2008 (2.9 a Year) and a Force of 'Approximately Sixty-Four' (3 Yuan, 13 Song, 19 Ming, 7 Romeo, 12 Kilo, 2 Shang, 4 Han, 1 Xia, 2–3 Jin) (pp. 8–9, Notes 25–35)
rows.usage: Gives the capability context for the transit, drawing on CRS (O'Rourke, Oct 2008), Jane's and Barabanov.
rows.finding: Verified by internal arithmetic (`ok`): 3 + 13 + 19 + 7 + 12 = 54 diesel boats; + 2 Shang + 4 Han = 60; + 1 Xia = 61; + 2 or 3 Jin = 63–64, matching 'approximately sixty-four'; 38 boats over the 13 intervals from 1995 to 2008 is 2.9 a year, as stated. Note 25 explains that the total counts only warfare-capable classes, and the Han 'commissioned in January 1980' dating follows Jane's though other sources date the lead boat to 1974.

rows.source: Tsugaru Strait Geometry: 'Roughly Eight Nautical Miles Wide at Its Narrowest' and a 'High Seas Corridor About Three Nautical Miles Wide' (pp. 1–2, Notes 9–11)
rows.usage: Illustrates how Japan limited its territorial sea to 3 nm in five straits to leave a corridor of high-seas freedoms for the October 2008 PLAN transit.
rows.finding: Numerical inconsistency and understatement (`fix`): a strait 8 nm wide with two 3-nm territorial belts leaves a corridor of 2 nm, not 'about three'; the strait's narrowest crossing (Tappi Misaki to Shirakami Misaki) is about 19.5 km, roughly 10.5 nm, which with 3-nm belts leaves roughly 4.5 nm. The legal argument is unaffected, but both figures cannot be right.

rows.source: USNS Bowditch Confrontations in the Yellow Sea EEZ ('March 2000 and Again in September 2002') and the Chinese Foreign Ministry's 'Relevant Rights' Statement (pp. 19–20, Notes 77–79)
rows.usage: Contrasts China's insistence on coastal-state control of survey activity in its own EEZ with the Han's covert passage through Japan's territorial sea.
rows.finding: Date error (`fix`): the first *Bowditch* confrontation occurred in **March 2001** (a Chinese frigate approached the survey ship in the Yellow Sea; this was followed by the April 2001 EP-3 collision, and the study's own Note 77 is headed 'Before EP-3'), not March 2000; the September 2002 confrontation and the 26 September 2002 Foreign Ministry statement referring to China's 'relevant rights' are correctly cited.

rows.source: Law-of-the-Sea Citations: UNCLOS Articles 19, 25, 30, 37–40, 245 and 38.3, Corfu Channel (1949), Japan's 1977/1996 Territorial Sea Laws, and China's and Japan's 1996 Accessions (pp. 11–15, 19–20, Notes 38–55, 73–82)
rows.usage: Provides the legal basis for treating the Han's passage as a violation of Japanese sovereignty and for assessing which passage regime applied.
rows.finding: Verified with quotation and date slips (`ok · slip`): Article 245 ('exclusive right to regulate, authorize and conduct marine scientific research'), Article 25(1), Article 30, Article 38(3), the *Corfu Channel* judgment (ICJ, 9 April 1949, the Court's first contentious case), China's accession on 7 June 1996 and Japan's on 20 June 1996 are accurate. Article 40 is quoted as 'prior consent of the coastal State' where the text reads 'prior authorization of the States bordering straits,' Article 19(2)(c) omits 'or security,' and the text dates Japan's 12-nm territorial sea to 1996 while Note 50 correctly attributes it to the 1977 law.

rows.source: Interpretive Claims: Navigational-Error Rebuttal (75–100 nm Off Course), '34 Submarine Passages in 2004 vs. 7 in 2003,' the Slow-Speed 'JMSDF Probing' Reading and Suo Nada 1983 Mine Exercises (pp. 17–23, Notes 69–70, 86–87, 96–101)
rows.usage: Supports the scouting, signaling and gatekeeping hypotheses with bathymetry, Japanese press counts, Chinese military writings and Japanese reporting on the submarine's behavior.
rows.finding:
**Open-claim evidence follow-up, November 22, 2026 — Reviewed; unresolved.** The supplied study's PDF p. 29 attributes the thirty-four-versus-seven statistic to a single Asahi Shimbun account, November 12, 2004, identified in note 86 on PDF p. 39. That narrows the missing source to a named edition. It does not supply an independently reproducible patrol series. The chart-based distance, translated strategic writings and explanations of signaling remain distinct components; consistency of the narrative does not verify any one of them. The author offers hypotheses rather than a demonstrated intent finding.

**Remaining gap or scope limit.** The November 12 Asahi passage and its counting rule; chart/route measurement and originals for the separately quoted strategic texts.

**Earlier audit record (preserved).** Plausible but not independently verifiable (`unk`): the 34-vs.-7 passage statistic comes from a single *Asahi Shimbun* item (Note 86), the 75–100 nm course deviation is drawn from the author's reading of a chart (INT 509) and the 'slow speed and erratic course' inference from Japanese press reports (Notes 100–101); the Chinese strategic-writing quotations (Notes 97–99, 107) were translated by a colleague and could not be re-checked. The three hypotheses are offered as possibilities and the study does not choose among them.

rows.source: EEZ freedoms, marine research consent and survey classification
rows.usage: The note is attached to: “While these tests would have been contrary to international law if performed in China’s territorial sea, the waters in which the tests were being performed were within the PRC exclusive economic zone, where international law provides all states the right to exercise high seas freedoms, including conducting scientific research, such as hydrographic surveys, not related to the natural resources of the zone.”
rows.finding: UNCLOS Article 58 extends specified high-seas freedoms and related lawful uses to the EEZ. Article 246 separately sets a consent regime for marine scientific research in the EEZ. It does not follow that all research unrelated to resources is automatically exempt. The treaty-text check establishes this distinction. Whether the particular activity was a hydrographic survey or marine scientific research requires separate evidence. Rechecked November 14, 2026. The local source PDF p. 28 expressly includes non-resource scientific research among its asserted EEZ freedoms. Article 246(2) requires coastal-state consent for marine scientific research in the EEZ, even where the test for discretionary refusal under 246(5)(a) may be absent. The incident-specific classification remains open.

rows.source: Similar-convenience routes: Articles 36 and 38(1)
rows.usage: Paraphrase of extracted passage, CMS02-N051: The passage cites Article 36 for a seaward route of similar convenience that avoids passage through the strait.
rows.finding: Reviewed November 11, 2026. The cited provision and described geography differ. Article 36 concerns a high-seas or EEZ route through the strait. Article 38(1) supplies the seaward-route exception for a strait formed by an island and the mainland of the bordering State. Retain that geographic condition when correcting the citation. The treaty comparison does not verify how Japan or China construed a particular strait.

rows.source: China’s warship passage declaration accompanied ratification
rows.usage: Paraphrase of extracted passage, CMS02-N061. The paper describes China’s accession documents as including a declaration on innocent passage.
rows.finding: Reviewed November 12, 2026. The UN lists China as having signed and ratified the Convention, with its declaration made upon ratification. Paragraph 4 asserts coastal-state authority to require advance approval or prior notification for passage by foreign warships. This is China’s stated interpretation. Correct accession to ratification.
evidence: UN Treaty Collection, China participant entry and declaration, paragraph 4

rows.source: UNCLOS protections against non-innocent passage
rows.usage: Paraphrase of extracted passage, CMS02-N080. Notes 80–81 describe a coastal state’s powers regarding non-innocent passage and noncomplying warships.
rows.finding: Reviewed November 12, 2026. Article 25(1) permits necessary steps in the territorial sea to prevent non-innocent passage. Article 30 permits requiring a warship to leave immediately after it disregards a request to comply with applicable coastal laws and regulations on passage. This verifies the sequence and scope stated in the passage.

rows.source: Territorial-sea research authority and surveys during transit passage
rows.usage: Paraphrase of extracted passage, CMS02-N073. Notes 73–74 describe exclusive coastal authority over marine scientific research in the territorial sea and consent for surveys during transit passage.
rows.finding: Reviewed November 12, 2026. Article 245 grants the coastal state exclusive authority to regulate, authorize, and conduct marine scientific research in its territorial sea and requires express consent. Article 40 separately requires prior authorization for research or survey activity by foreign ships during transit passage, including hydrographic survey ships.

rows.source: Continuous and expeditious passage and its exceptions
rows.usage: Paraphrase of extracted passage, CMS02-N042. Note 42 defines innocent passage as continuous, expeditious transit that is not prejudicial to the coastal state’s peace, order, or security.
rows.finding: Reviewed November 13, 2026. Articles 18 and 19 supply both elements. Article 18(2) includes stopping and anchoring when incidental to ordinary navigation, required by force majeure or distress, or necessary for rendering assistance. The definition is supported when those express exceptions are retained.

rows.source: Territorial sea versus waters landward of a baseline
rows.usage: Paraphrase of extracted passage, CMS02-N039. The extracted passage calls enclosed waters the territorial sea.
rows.finding: Reviewed November 13, 2026. Article 3 limits breadth to twelve nautical miles measured from the applicable baselines. paper_memo.memo_title: Analytical & Source-Audit Memo: CMS-02 — Scouting, Signaling, and Gatekeeping (Peter A. Dutton, CMSI, 2009)

sections.heading: 1. Strategic Context & Core Thesis
sections.body: China Maritime Study No. 2 reads the **PLAN's operations around the Japanese archipelago through international law**. Peter Dutton, a retired Navy judge advocate, notes that China's flotilla transits (Tsugaru, October 2008) and submarine movements (Osumi 2003, the George Washington shadowing of 2008) are largely carefully lawful — they stay in Japan's 'high seas corridors' — and contrasts them with the **10 November 2004 submerged transit of a Han-class nuclear attack submarine through the Ishigaki Strait**, which both Beijing's and Tokyo's doctrines treat as a violation. He offers three explanations (scouting, signaling, and testing Japan's antisubmarine 'gates') and concludes that, whatever the intent, the Han episode weakened China's own legal campaign for coastal-state control over foreign military activity.

sections.heading: 2. Section-by-Section Analytical Breakdown
sections.body:
• **Introduction and Table 1 (pp. 1–7)**: The Tsugaru flotilla, earlier transits and the incident chronology.
• **The Chinese Submarine Fleet (pp. 8–9)**: A 64-boat inventory by class.
• **Japanese Geography and the Law of the Sea (pp. 9–15)**: Ishigaki–Tarama–Miyako geometry, innocent vs. transit passage, the five Japanese straits, *Corfu Channel* and the U.S. view.
• **Chinese Legal Perspectives (pp. 15–17)**: PLA guidance on straits, the 1992 Territorial Sea law, EEZ restrictions and China's 'regret.'
• **Strategic Implications (pp. 17–24)**: Technical error, scouting, signaling and gatekeeping.
• **Conclusions (pp. 25–27)**: Legal effect, relative gains and losses, and the delegitimization strategy.

sections.heading: 3. Key Doctrinal Concepts, Terminology & Quantitative Claims
sections.body:
• **Concepts**: *transit passage* vs. *innocent passage*, *international strait*, *high seas corridor*, *route of similar convenience*, *useful route* vs. *necessary route*, *scouting–signaling–gatekeeping*, *first island chain*, coastal-state control of the EEZ.
• **Quantitative claims**: `38` submarines commissioned 1995–2008 (`2.9` a year); `~64` submarines; `4` ships in the 19 Oct 2008 flotilla; the Han submerged at `~100 m` for `~2 hours`; strait widths `8 nm` (Tsugaru) and corridor `~3 nm`; Tarama `18.2 nm` from Ishigaki and `<24 nm` from Miyako; `34` submarine passages in 2004 vs `7` in 2003; Chunxiao field `~2 km` from the Japanese-claimed EEZ boundary; China's `7 June 1996` and Japan's `20 June 1996` UNCLOS accessions.

sections.heading: 4. Audit Assessment & Analytical Significance
sections.body:
Of the 6 reference rows audited in `CMS-02`, 3 are rated `ok` (one with quotation and date slips), 1 is `unk` and **2 are rated `fix` (`[CMS02-R03]`, `[CMS02-R04]`)**:
• **`[CMS02-R03]` (`fix` — Tsugaru Strait Geometry)**: The 8-nm width and 3-nm corridor figures cannot both hold; the narrowest crossing is about 10.5 nm.
• **`[CMS02-R04]` (`fix` — Bowditch Dates)**: The first confrontation was in March 2001, not 2000.
• **`[CMS02-R05]` (`ok · slip` — UNCLOS Quotations and Japanese Law Dates)**: Article 40 and Article 19(2)(c) are not quoted verbatim, and the date of Japan's 12-nm law is inconsistent with Note 50.

The study's **legal framework is sound and still the standard reference** for how the Han incident is taught; the slips are all in secondary facts. Its most lasting contribution is the 'scouting–signaling–gatekeeping' typology, which later CMSI work on far-seas operations extends from submarines to carrier and surface-group transits.

**Footnote rows**: all 107 footnotes were extracted and consolidated into 79 source rows in the Reference Audit Matrix (CMS02-N001 to CMS02-N109). Repeat citations of the same source within this paper, including Ibid. and short-form notes, share one row, which lists each note's passage and result. Footnote-level result: 107 notes: 50 (47%) are confirmed, 1 of them against a retrieved source and 49 after an outside web search (44 of the latter with a slip or an unchecked detail noted); 6 are flagged for reader check; 57 (53%) are not confirmed. Of the 57 notes not confirmed, 7 are Chinese-language sources that have not been searched in Chinese (a search in Chinese could settle some of them); 1 was judged not web-checkable (1 print-only book or paywalled item); 49 were searched on the web without finding corroboration. A source row is `ok` only when every note in it is confirmed, and `fix` when a note is confirmed wrong; the paper's 79 source rows are 31 `ok`, 0 `fix` and 48 `unk`. Notes flagged for reader check, for example (the outside search found something a reader should look at; none is a finding that the author is wrong): `CMS02-N001`: The sentence says the October 2008 transit came a month after Prime Minister Shinzo Abe stepped down and the more hawkish Taro Aso took office. The sources retrieved show Aso taking office on 24 September 2008 after Yasuo Fukuda, who had succeeded Abe in September 2007; Abe's own resignation date was not stated in the results; `CMS02-N025`: The sentence says the PLAN commissioned about thirty-eight new submarines between 1995 and 2008, an average of 2.9 a year. O'Rourke's 2009 testimony counts 26 domestic submarines from 1995 to 2007 (2.0 a year), excluding the 12 Kilos; adding the Kilos gives 38 over 1995 to 2007 (2.9 a year over thirteen years), so the stated…; `CMS02-N031`: The sentence says the first Han was not commissioned until January 1980; Wikipedia and Britannica say the first boat (hull 401) entered service in 1974 and give December 1980 for the second hull; and 3 more. 22 notes carry a reader note on how the note is displayed or cited.

paper_memo.memo_title: Analytical & Source-Audit Memo: CMS-15 — Echelon Defense: The Role of Sea Power in Chinese Maritime Dispute Strategy (Ryan D. Martinson, CMSI, 2018)

sections.heading: 1. Strategic Context & Core Thesis
sections.body: China Maritime Study No. 15 gives a name and a structure to the way China pursues its maritime claims short of war. Ryan Martinson argues that since 2006 Beijing has built an **echelon defense system** (梯次防卫体系): coast guard cutters — white hulls — operate on the front line under cover of routine law enforcement and use verbal threats and nonlethal force but never armed force, while the PLA Navy — gray hulls — keeps a second line that deters escalation by the claimant state and intervention by the United States. The model exploits two asymmetries (power and resolve), serves the dual goals of 'rights protection' and 'stability maintenance,' and by 2016 had expanded Chinese control over the East and South China Seas at little cost in violence. The monograph is based largely on Chinese-language official, military and academic sources, and a decade-by-decade comparison of 2006 and 2016.

sections.heading: 2. Section-by-Section Analytical Breakdown
sections.body:
• **Introduction: Echelon Defense in Action (pp. 1–5)**: Scarborough Shoal 2012 as the model case.
• **Part 1: China's Blue National Territory (pp. 5–11)**: Territorial and maritime-rights disputes, the nine-dash line, and why the claims matter.
• **Part 2: White Hulls, Gray Hulls (pp. 11–26)**: CMS, FLE, CMP, the 2013 CCG reform, force structure (Table 1, Figure 3), legal bases (Table 2) and the PLAN surface fleet (Table 3).
• **Part 3: Sea Power and Strategy (pp. 27–32)**: Rights vs. stability, 'one-plus,' incrementalism, and four functions of sea power (Table 4).
• **Part 4: Echelon Defense (pp. 32–49)**: Six operations: sovereignty patrol, blockade, tracking and monitoring, obstruction and eviction, escort (Table 5) and support and cover (Table 6).
• **Part 5: New Frontiers (pp. 49–59)**: Presence and enforcement in 2006 vs. 2016, four decisions, and the costs of coercion.

sections.heading: 3. Key Doctrinal Concepts, Terminology & Quantitative Claims
sections.body:
• **Concepts**: *echelon defense system*, *white hulls / gray hulls*, *rights protection* (维权) vs. *stability maintenance* (维稳), *blue national territory*, *historic rights*, *one-plus strategy*, *bubu weiying*, *administrative control*, *support and cover*, 'war without gun smoke.'
• **Quantitative claims**: `3 million km²` of claimed jurisdiction (`2 million km²` in the South China Sea); `28` CMS and `12` FLE cutters over 1,000 tons (end 2012); `>120` CCG cutters over 1,000 tons (early 2017); `12,000`-ton Zhaotou class; `36` provincial cutters (600–1,500 tons); `23` PLAN surface ships commissioned in 2016 (US: `6`); `113` / `212,242 nm` CMS patrols (2008), `347` / `543,652 nm` (2013); `76` utility boats and `20` trawlers at Scarborough (22 May 2012); Senkaku formations of `3–5` ships at two-week intervals; `20` cutters escorting `several hundred` trawlers (Aug 2016); Luconia Shoals `~90 nm` from Malaysia.

sections.heading: 4. Audit Assessment & Analytical Significance
sections.body:
Of the 6 reference rows audited in `CMS-15`, 5 are rated `ok` (two with table or timing slips) and 1 is rated `unk`; no substantive `fix` was found:
• **`[CMS15-R02]` (`ok · slip` — Table 3 Hull Number)**: Honghu and Luomahu are both printed as hull 963; Luomahu is 964.
• **`[CMS15-R04]` (`unk` — Patrol Statistics)**: The 2008, 2012 and 2013 patrol figures mix national and South China Sea scopes and cannot be traced to their Chinese sources.
• **`[CMS15-R05]` (`ok · slip` — Indonesian Incidents)**: The incidents check out; the text's 'four months' and 'failed to prevent' language do not match the table.

The monograph is the **definitive English-language account of the white-hull / gray-hull division of labor**: its core claims (the 2012 Scarborough template, the CCG buildup, the four decisions) are well sourced from primary Chinese materials and have been reinforced by events since 2018. Its limitations are the ones the author acknowledges — Chinese policy documents are read through speeches and journal articles, and the text stops at early 2017, before the CCG's transfer to the Central Military Commission.

**Footnote rows**: all 353 footnotes were extracted and consolidated into 318 source rows in the Reference Audit Matrix (CMS15-N001 to CMS15-N353). Repeat citations of the same source within this paper, including Ibid. and short-form notes, share one row, which lists each note's passage and result. Footnote-level result: 353 notes: 106 (30%) are confirmed, 1 of them against a retrieved source and 105 after an outside web search (88 of the latter with a slip or an unchecked detail noted); 8 are flagged for reader check; 247 (70%) are not confirmed. A source row is `ok` only when every note in it is confirmed, and `fix` when a note is confirmed wrong; the paper's 318 source rows are 97 `ok`, 0 `fix` and 221 `unk`. Notes flagged for reader check, for example (the outside search found something a reader should look at; none is a finding that the author is wrong): `CMS15-N221`: The sentence says China charged four Japanese citizens working on WWII-era chemical disposal with espionage, and the note says they were freed a few days after Zhan Qixiong (released 24 Sept 2010); `CMS15-N261`: The sentence's account of the 20 March 2013 Paracels incident (a Chinese ship, identified as the Type 037 subchaser Wanning, firing on a Vietnamese fishing boat) rests on Vietnam's account; `CMS15-N266`: The note says that in May 2010 CMS 51 tracked and verbally harassed a Japanese survey ship, as one of at least three such East China Sea incidents in 2010 to 2012. paper_memo.memo_title: Analytical & Source-Audit Memo: CMS-16 — Chinese Nationalism and the 'Gray Zone' (Andrew Chubb, CMSI, 2021)

sections.heading: 1. Strategic Context & Core Thesis
sections.body: China Maritime Study No. 16 tests a popular explanation of China's assertiveness at sea — that **popular nationalism** pushes Beijing to act — against nine case studies of 'gray-zone' coercion between 2006 and 2014. Andrew Chubb finds little evidence of bottom-up pressure on decisions: the state often avoided publicizing its actions (the 2007 Triton 626 clash, the 2009 *Impeccable* harassment, the 2014 HYSY 981 deployment), nationalist surges tended to follow rather than precede the operations, and each case has sufficient cause in administrative capabilities, resource value, legal change, perceived challenges to China's claims and elite politics. Public opinion mattered, at most, in three cases (Indonesia fisheries, Scarborough 2012, the Diaoyu nationalization), and even there the party-state may have acted the same way. The implication is that China's maritime behavior reflects calculated policy that outside actors can try to deter.

sections.heading: 2. Section-by-Section Analytical Breakdown
sections.body:
• **Introduction (pp. 1–10)**: Question, definitions, alternative explanations and method.
• **Case Study 1: White Hulls and 'Special Operations' (pp. 11–17)**: Regular patrols from July 2006, Triton 626 (June 2007) and interference with Vietnamese surveys.
• **Case Studies 2–4 (pp. 18–38)**: *Impeccable* (2009), Sino-Indonesian fisheries (2010–16) and the Diaoyu fishing clash (2010).
• **Case Studies 5–6 (pp. 39–57)**: Reed Bank and the cable cuttings (2011); Scarborough Shoal (2012).
• **Case Studies 7–9 (pp. 58–76)**: The Diaoyu nationalization (2012); Second Thomas Shoal (2013–14); HYSY 981 (2014).
• **Conclusion (pp. 76–79)**: Where public opinion mattered, and policy implications for dialogue, incident handling and deterrence.

sections.heading: 3. Key Doctrinal Concepts, Terminology & Quantitative Claims
sections.body:
• **Concepts**: *popular nationalism / nationalist public opinion*, *gray zone*, *party-state*, *state behavior vs. foreign policy* (对外政策), *rights defense and stability maintenance* (维权维稳), *special rights-defense operations*, *strategic channeling*, *feedback loop*, *maritime consciousness* (海洋意识).
• **Quantitative claims**: `9` case studies (`3` with plausible popular influence); regular patrols from `July 2006` covering `3 million km²` by `December 2007`; Triton 626 clash `47 nm` west of Triton Island (`29–30 June 2007`); *Impeccable* `~75 nm` from Hainan, `5` Chinese vessels (`8 March 2009`); BSI `4,400` (17 March 2009) and `1,100 → 9,000+` (7 September 2010); Captain Zhan detained `17 days`; HYSY 981 `120 nm` from Vietnam, `17 nm` south of Triton, `171` alleged rammings; `23` figures; about `306` endnotes.

sections.heading: 4. Audit Assessment & Analytical Significance
sections.body:
Of the 6 reference rows audited in `CMS-16`, 4 are rated `ok` (one with a direction slip), 1 is `unk` and **1 is rated `fix` (`[CMS16-R01]`)**:
• **`[CMS16-R01]` (`fix` — 'Three' vs. 'Four Most Plausible' Cases)**: The headline finding says three cases show plausible nationalist influence, but the policy section refers to 'three of the four most plausible cases,' which implies a fourth (the 2010 Diaoyu captain case) that the study excludes.
• **`[CMS16-R02]` (`ok · slip` — Impeccable)**: The ship was south, not east, of Hainan; the rest of the account checks out.
• **`[CMS16-R06]` (`unk` — Baidu Search Index)**: The central quantitative proxy is a proprietary series that appears mostly as images.

The monograph's method is its strength: it asks, case by case, whether the **state publicized the action before, during or after** and uses the contrast between Chinese- and English-language coverage to infer motive. Its weakness is the one the author acknowledges — the BSI measures attention, not sentiment, and the sample covers only on-water coercion — so the conclusion that nationalism did not drive ship movements is better supported than the broader claim that popular sentiment did not shape China's diplomacy at all.

**Footnote rows**: all 317 footnotes were extracted and consolidated into 271 source rows in the Reference Audit Matrix (CMS16-S4N001 to CMS16-N313). Repeat citations of the same source within this paper, including Ibid. and short-form notes, share one row, which lists each note's passage and result. Footnote-level result: 317 notes: 110 (35%) are confirmed, 1 of them against a retrieved source and 109 after an outside web search (94 of the latter with a slip or an unchecked detail noted); 6 are flagged for reader check; 207 (65%) are not confirmed. Of the 207 notes not confirmed, 40 are Chinese-language sources that have not been searched in Chinese (a search in Chinese could settle some of them); 40 were judged not web-checkable (2 notes that are fragments or run-on text attached to a Chinese-language source; 16 the authors' own data, imagery or analysis; 2 private interviews or conversations; 10 notes that are explanatory text or a fragment, not a citation; 10 other items); 127 were searched on the web without finding corroboration. A source row is `ok` only when every note in it is confirmed, and `fix` when a note is confirmed wrong; the paper's 271 source rows are 93 `ok`, 0 `fix` and 178 `unk`. Notes flagged for reader check, for example (the outside search found something a reader should look at; none is a finding that the author is wrong): `CMS16-N062`: The sentence says Haijian 51 (commissioned November 2005) was identified as ramming Vietnamese geological survey ships later in the year (citing a Vietnamese researcher interviewed by e-mail); `CMS16-N064`: The sentence says Impeccable was about seventy-five nautical miles east of Hainan Island according to the Pentagon; search results quoting the Garamone/American Forces Press Service report say 75 miles south of Hainan (other outlets say about 70 miles south); `CMS16-N093`: The footnote says the PRC's interception of a U.S. EP-3 over the South China Sea in April 2001 occurred four months into George W. Bush's presidency. The collision was on 1 April 2001, and Bush took office on 20 January 2001, which is about ten weeks (a little over two months); and 3 more. 95 notes carry a reader note on how the note is displayed or cited.

rows.source: The 2016 Natuna and South Luconia Incidents: CCG 3304 Ramming on 20 March, MMEA Expulsion of 100+ Fishing Vessels on 24 March, Indonesian Navy Detentions in May–June and Jokowi's Cabinet Meeting Aboard KRI Imam Bonjol (Introduction, pp. 1–3, Notes 1–11)
rows.usage: Frames the study with the sequence of March–June 2016 events that revealed China's southward claims and Indonesia's willingness to arrest Chinese vessels.
rows.finding: Verified, with a cross-document match (`ok`): the 20 March ramming by CCG 3304, the detention of the crew by Indonesian fisheries officers, the 27 May and 17 June naval actions (shots fired, one crewman injured) and the cabinet meeting aboard *Imam Bonjol* match press reports and Martinson's Table 5 in `CMS-15` (20 March, 27 May, 17 June). The three events span about three months, as Bentley says ('third maritime incident in three months'), whereas `CMS-15` describes them as occurring 'in four months.' The 24 March MMEA announcement of a fleet of 100-plus vessels rests on Malaysian press and ministerial statements that were not re-pulled.

rows.source: BAKAMLA Build-Up: Table 1 (1 Tanjung Datu + 3 Pulau Nipah + 6 Bintang Laut = 10 Ships), $56 Million Supplement (Feb 2015) and Personnel 'to Two Thousand . . . a Fivefold Increase' (Indonesia chapter, pp. 35–37, Table 1, Notes 171–183)
rows.usage: Shows that Indonesia's coast guard agency has been given larger ships, more funding and personnel to patrol the Natuna waters.
rows.finding: Verified by internal cross-check (`ok`): Table 1 lists 1 + 3 + 6 = 10 ships, which matches the text (one 110-m *Tanjung Datu* commissioned January 2018; three 80-m *Pulau Nipah* ships launched December 2018; six 48-m *Bintang Laut* craft launched 2013–2015, the third in February 2014 and the fourth to sixth in 2015); and a personnel total of 2,000 as a 'fivefold increase' implies a previous strength of about 400. The $56 million appropriation and the personnel projection come from Indonesian press and parliamentary sources (Notes 171–172) that were not re-checked.

rows.source: Surveillance Ship Directorate (DKP): About 35 Patrol Ships, 2013 Budget of ~$16 Million, Western Command with 13 Vessels on 'Barely Exceeding $6 Million', Fewer Than 1,000 Personnel (Indonesia chapter, pp. 37–38, Notes 186–193)
rows.usage: Describes Indonesia's original maritime law-enforcement agency in the South China Sea as understaffed and underfunded.
rows.finding: Verified by internal arithmetic (`ok`): the Western Command's 13 of about 35 vessels (37%) and just over $6 million of a $16 million budget (about 38%) are mutually consistent, supporting the claim of a proportional split; the 2013 budget and personnel figures (fewer than 1,000, 57 at Pontianak) come from Indonesian sources (Notes 188–193) that were not re-pulled, and the ship count dates to a later year than the 2013 budget it is paired with.

rows.source: MMEA Force Size and Plans: ~130 Vessels / 8 Aircraft / 5,369 Personnel (2018) vs. 228 Vessels / 9,400 Personnel / 15 Rotary + 12 Fixed-Wing Aircraft by 2040; Table 2 Inventory (Malaysia chapter, pp. 72–74, Table 2, Notes 377–386)
rows.usage: Quantifies Malaysia's coast guard expansion in response to Chinese pressure and cites Admiral Zulkifili's call for multipurpose mother ships.
rows.finding: Verified with table slips (`ok · slip`): the planned growth is internally proportional — vessels 130 → 228 (×1.75), personnel 5,369 → 9,400 (×1.75) and aircraft 8 → 27 (×3.4) — and Table 2 sums to 2 + 2 + 15 + 15 + 2 = 36 primary platforms (WPC and larger). Table 2's note column gives a '157 mm main gun' for a 75-m, 1,300-ton ship (57 mm is the plausible calibre), and the text's 'three Bagan Datuk-class' patrol ships commissioned do not appear in the table's class list.

rows.source: China's 'Firsts' Near Natuna: Traditional Fishing Grounds (March 2016), Overlapping Claims with Indonesia (June 2016), 'Historic Rights' (July 2016) and Historic Fishing Rights (December 2019) (Introduction, pp. 6–7, Notes 15–20)
rows.usage: Documents the escalation of China's declaratory claims in the southernmost nine-dash-line waters.
rows.finding:
**Open-claim evidence follow-up, November 22, 2026 — Reviewed; unresolved.** The June 2016 Foreign Ministry statement explicitly combines traditional fishing grounds with overlapping claims to maritime rights and interests. The March 23 briefing says China had stated its position to Indonesia and rejects the question's territorial-sovereignty framing. These passages corroborate dated formulations, not their first-ever use. The Indonesian Cabinet account is evidence of the protest, not of priority in China's own vocabulary. Establishing the March and December firsts still requires the precise contemporary statements and a search of earlier official usage. Do not infer those firsts from the later ministry migration date embedded in the June page's URL.

**Remaining gap or scope limit.** Original March 21 and December 2019 statements plus earlier-use comparison sufficient to establish each claimed first.

**Earlier audit record (preserved).** Unverified and in tension with other sources (`unk`): the 12 July 2016 government statement that China has 'historic rights' in the South China Sea is documented, but 'for the first time' is hard to reconcile with Article 14 of China's 1998 Exclusive Economic Zone and Continental Shelf Law (which reserves 'historic rights') and with Martinson's account in `CMS-15` that China has long claimed 'some brand of historic rights' without defining them. The March 2016 'traditional fishing grounds' statement and December 2019 Chinese Foreign Ministry language were not re-pulled from the cited MFA transcripts. Source recheck. A June 2016 Foreign Ministry statement expressly joins a traditional-fishing-grounds claim with overlapping claims to maritime rights and interests. This establishes the language and its use by June. Its priority relative to other official statements still requires the March 2016 and December 2019 transcripts and earlier contemporaneous records. Source recheck. Indonesia’s cabinet account independently dates its diplomatic protest and characterization of its position to March 21, 2016. The Chinese transcript recovered from March 23 confirms that Beijing had stated its position to Jakarta. China’s June written statement contains both formulations. The archived 21 March Chinese transcript and a search of earlier official usage remain necessary to substantiate historical priority.
evidence: Chinese Foreign Ministry, Hua Chunying’s June 2016 statement
PRC Foreign Ministry regular briefing, March 23
Chinese Foreign Ministry, June 2016 statement, traditional fishing grounds and overlapping claims paragraph
Chinese Foreign Ministry, March 23, 2016 briefing, Indonesia questions

rows.usage: Underpins the argument that China's reach is stretched at the far southern end of the nine-dash line.
rows.finding: Verified (`ok`): great-circle estimates agree — Hainan's southern tip is about 850 nm from Natuna Besar and about 800 nm from the South Luconia Shoals, so 'over 700 nm' is a conservative statement; the 2017 and 2018 withdrawals from Vietnam's blocks near Vanguard Bank under Chinese pressure and Vietnam's return in 2018–19 match reporting at the time. The claims that 'at least three CCG vessels' escorted survey ships a week before the July 2017 decision rest on AIS data (Note 47) that were not re-pulled.

rows.source: Malaysia’s individual role in U.S. entry to the East Asia Summit
rows.usage: Note 252 attributes a reversal of Malaysian policy and a decisive lobbying role to Malaysia.
rows.finding:
**Open-claim evidence follow-up, November 22, 2026 — Reviewed; unresolved.** The November 2010 U.S.–Malaysian press exchange directly records Malaysian support for greater U.S. engagement. The 2011 White House briefing describes Najib’s summit intervention on maritime principles. Neither demonstrates a prior Malaysian reversal or that its lobbying was decisive in the earlier collective invitation. The ASEAN documentary series establishes the institutional milestone without assigning individual causal weight.

**Remaining gap or scope limit.** Dated Malaysian policy records and diplomatic evidence for the claimed reversal and decisive lobbying role.

**Earlier audit record (preserved).** The September 2010 ASEAN–U.S. joint record documents the collective invitation, and the U.S. briefing describes the October 2010 appearance as participation as a guest of the chair. Neither record establishes Malaysia’s earlier position, a reversal, or its individual influence on other members. Those assertions need a Malaysian statement or a diplomatic account of the negotiations. Rechecked November 14, 2026. Read the September 24 joint record against the contemporaneous October account and the next year's EAS briefing. The invitation is attributable to ASEAN collectively, and Malaysia is identified as an early speaker in 2011. Neither event establishes an individual lobbying role in 2010. A record of Malaysia's position before the invitation and of the member consultations is still needed. Follow-up review, November 14, 2026. ASEAN’s own document series records the collective decision and schedule for entry. A Malaysian role is compatible with that account, but the public joint record does not show the reported reversal or measure one member’s influence. Follow-up review, November 15, 2026. The fifth summit’s chairman’s statement records the collective decision on U.S. and Russian participation. The subsequent Clinton–Anifah remarks document bilateral support and discussion. Neither is evidence that Malaysia reversed a former position or was decisive in winning agreement. Source recheck. The July 2010 joint communiqué establishes that ASEAN foreign ministers had already agreed to recommend formal invitations to Russia and the United States before the fifth summit. It supplies the earlier collective milestone and does not identify Malaysia’s position before the decision or show that its lobbying was decisive. Dated Malaysian statements or diplomatic records remain necessary.
evidence: White House 2011 EAS briefing, order of interventions
ASEAN, East Asia Summit document series
ASEAN foreign ministers’ joint communiqué, July 2010

rows.source: Central Luconia: discovery history and F23 production start
rows.usage: The note is attached to: “Malaysia began developing offshore hydrocarbons in disputed areas near Luconia (e.g., the F field) in the mid-1980s, following earlier discoveries in the area dating back another decade.”
rows.finding: A Sarawak Shell technical paper dates F23 coming on stream to 1983, and JOGMEC traces discoveries in the Central Luconia field group to 1968 onward. The paper’s mid-1980s date is too late if it refers to development of the field group, since F23 was already producing in 1983. A narrower claim about a specific later field should name the field and milestone.

rows.source: Indonesia IMET: restrictions, limited programme activity and 2005 certification
rows.usage: Note 209 describes the interruption of U.S.–Indonesia engagement and uses 2005 as the endpoint.
rows.finding: The February 2005 State Department statement establishes the decision to certify Indonesia for regular IMET. Archived U.S. training material from before 2001 distinguishes the expanded programme from full IMET. The claim of a complete decade-long cessation needs the programme and years specified. The 2005 certification alone does not date the restoration of every form of bilateral military cooperation. Rechecked November 14, 2026. Distinguish the period of restrictions from the continuity of expanded IMET and the two 2005 decisions. Regular IMET certification came in February. The November national-security waiver concerned Foreign Military Financing and related restrictions. A single end date for a complete suspension collapses different U.S. programs and authorities.
evidence: State Department IMET certification statement, February 2005
Archived U.S. regional training programme material
Congressional Research Service RL31672, military restrictions and 2005 decisions

rows.source: Malaysia’s 2017 GDP growth and Indonesia’s military-spending measure
rows.usage: Note 64 reports Malaysia’s 5.9% real growth and Indonesia’s roughly $8.2 billion defence budget in 2017.
rows.finding:
**Open-claim evidence follow-up, November 22, 2026 — Reviewed; unresolved.** The original and revised Indonesian budget documents distinguish defense-function and defense-ministry allocations. Converting one of them to US$8.2 billion requires a budget stage and exchange-rate convention. The Malaysian central-bank page was blocked during this check. Neither a later expenditure database nor an arbitrary currency conversion verifies the exact ADIO figures cited.

**Remaining gap or scope limit.** The ADIO 2017 budget measure and conversion method; an accessible dated Malaysian 2017 growth release.

**Earlier audit record (preserved).** Bank Negara Malaysia reports full-year growth of 5.9%. SIPRI’s military-expenditure series and the World Bank’s current-dollar presentation measure spending, which can differ from an authorized budget. Without the underlying ADIO table and a defined exchange-rate basis, the $8.2 billion figure is not established as comparable to SIPRI’s expenditure series. Rechecked November 14, 2026. Indonesia's defense ministry reported the original 2017 ministry allocation at Rp108 trillion while discussing a revised budget request in July. That allocation implies a conversion of about Rp13,170 per dollar for $8.2 billion. Cite the budget stage and rate explicitly. The cited ADIO conversion method remains unavailable. Source recheck. Indonesia’s 2017 budget documents distinguish the defense function’s original Rp108.2938 trillion allocation from the defense ministry’s original Rp108.0118 trillion and revised Rp114.8232 trillion allocations. These primary amounts confirm why the dollar figure requires the ADIO series, budget stage and conversion date.
evidence: Bank Negara Malaysia 2017 fourth-quarter and full-year release
World Bank indicator, Indonesia military expenditure
Indonesian defense ministry, July 17, 2017, original APBN and revised-budget discussion

rows.usage: Note 264 attributes about 20% of 2016 government revenue to hydrocarbon production and development.
rows.finding: Malaysia’s Fiscal Updates 2017 reports RM34.6 billion in petroleum-related revenue in 2017, up 11.8% from 2016, implying roughly RM31 billion for 2016. rows.source: Fahru Zaini’s 2014 Natuna statement and the official dispute position
rows.usage: The note is attached to: “Fahru Zaini publicly acknowledged—for the first time in unequivocal language—that Indonesia had a dispute with China, stating that Beijing had “claimed Natuna waters as their territorial waters,” and that “this dispute will have a large impact on the security of the Natuna waters.””
rows.finding: The ISEAS study reproduces Zaini’s March 2014 remarks about China’s claim and its security implications. It also records Foreign Minister Natalegawa’s subsequent denial of a territorial dispute. The quotation is corroborated, while the characterization of it as Indonesia’s first unequivocal acknowledgement of a dispute requires a broader historical and institutional check. Rechecked November 14, 2026. Antara's contemporaneous March 19 reporting quotes a foreign-ministry official describing earlier objections about the map. That is evidence of earlier diplomatic objections and warrants narrowing the first-time claim. Date and attribute Zaini's remarks to him, and distinguish prior map objections and the foreign minister's subsequent position on a territorial dispute. Follow-up review, November 14, 2026. Antara’s March reporting and the ISEAS reconstruction identify a statement by Zaini and a subsequent different position from the foreign minister. Attribute each separately. The categorical wording first unequivocal acknowledgement by Indonesia requires broader evidence and should be removed or narrowed.
evidence: ISEAS study, pp. 29–30, Zaini and Natalegawa statements
Antara, March 19, 2014, foreign-ministry account of previous objections

rows.source: Naval War College faculty coverage of Southeast Asia at publication
rows.usage: The note is attached to: “For instance, while China studies are well represented at institutions such as the U.S. Naval War College, no current member of the institution’s faculty focuses on Southeast Asia.”
rows.finding: Official faculty biographies list Southeast Asia among the expertise or teaching areas of faculty including John Garofano and Paul Rasmussen. Rasmussen’s record also dates his Monterey appointment to 2022. A current directory cannot by itself reconstruct staffing and research focus when the monograph was written. A publication-date faculty roster and definition of focuses on are needed to test the historical claim. Consistency review, November 14, 2026. Garofano's 2021 CV dates his Naval War College professorship from 2016 and records Vietnam-focused scholarship. The monograph's surrounding paragraph is particularly concerned with Indonesia and Malaysia. Qualify the categorical claim about all of Southeast Asia, and support any narrower finding about Indonesia or Malaysia with a dated faculty survey.
evidence: U.S. Naval War College, Garofano CV, appointment and publications

rows.source: Five dragons analogy: narrower law enforcement versus broader actors
rows.usage: The note is attached to: “What amounts to an “Indonesian Coast Guard” today strongly resembles the previous chaos of China’s “five dragons” that existed before the formation of the CCG in 2013, in which multiple agencies with overlapping authorities were competing among themselves for limited resources.”
rows.finding: The cited 2012 ICG report organizes its discussion around nine dragons, covering a wider set of South China Sea policy actors. Martinson’s separate account explicitly uses the five-dragons model for maritime law enforcement before the 2013 reorganization. These are different scopes, so the numerical difference alone does not refute the analogy. Cite a source defining the five agencies and keep the Indonesia comparison identified as the author’s analytical judgment. Consistency review, November 14, 2026. Attribute the five-agency formulation to the narrower administrative account and the nine-actor formulation to ICG's wider grouping. State the Indonesian comparison as the report author's interpretation. The 2010 civilian-agency lists in CMS11-R13 provide institutional context, not a count for Indonesia.
evidence: ICG report record and full-report access
Martinson, creation of the China Coast Guard (indexed text; direct PDF currently unavailable)

rows.source: MMEA powers: correct the act year and cite sections
rows.usage: Notes 366–367 cite MMEA Act 2014 for armed-forces command in emergencies and vessel enforcement powers.
rows.finding: The law is the Malaysian Maritime Enforcement Agency Act 2004, Act 633, not an Act 2014. Section 17 provides for general armed-forces command and control of the agency or a ministerially determined part during emergency, special crisis or war. Section 7 sets out enforcement powers, including vessel expulsion, with relevant limitations. The substantive command provision is supported; correct the year and use section references because pagination differs between reprints.
evidence: Act 633, official-law reprint with 2018 amendments, sections 7 and 17

rows.source: Natuna fleet: episode confirmed, precise count not in cited article
rows.usage: The note is attached to: “Most recently, from December 2019 to January 2020, a large Chinese fishing fleet—over fifty ships—operated in the southern South China Sea, escorted by multiple CCG patrol ships.”
rows.finding:
**Open-claim evidence follow-up, November 22, 2026 — Reviewed; unresolved.** The retrieved January 5 Jakarta Post report confirms continued Chinese fishing activity with coastguard support. Its accessible text does not supply the over-fifty fleet count. An episode-wide tally can exceed a single observation, so a smaller snapshot would not alone disprove it; later repetitions also need an independent source chain.

**Remaining gap or scope limit.** A dated episode-wide observation or official fleet tally with unique vessels distinguished from repeated sightings.

**Earlier audit record (preserved).** The retrieved January 5 Jakarta Post article confirms continuing Chinese fishing activity and accompanying coastguard vessels, but does not quantify more than fifty fishing ships. Later congressional research reproduces that larger count, but its underlying provenance needs checking for independence. Keep the episode corroborated while tracing the precise fleet tally; a lower count from one observation does not alone disprove a larger episode-wide total.
