rows.source: June 2016 maritime-rights statement: avoid a boundary-negotiation overclaim
rows.usage: The note is attached to: “Following the June 2016 incident with Indonesian forces, China publicly declared for the first time in over two decades that it had overlapping maritime claims with Indonesia in the South China Sea, and that the two countries needed to negotiate their overlapping boundaries.”
rows.finding: The June 20 transcript expressly states overlapping claims for maritime rights and interests while denying a territorial-sovereignty dispute. It calls for communication and settlement of the issue, not expressly negotiation of overlapping boundaries. It also cannot establish first time in over two decades without a historical comparison. The existing flag discusses a March fishing-grounds claim, which is not the attached passage. Keep the June statement supported but qualify novelty and boundary-negotiation language. Rechecked November 14, 2026. The June 20 answer to the follow-up question supports this narrower wording: China said the countries had overlapping claims to maritime rights and interests in part of the South China Sea and called for constructive communication to settle the issue. A boundary-negotiation demand and the claim of historical novelty each need separate evidence.
evidence: Original June 20, 2016 transcript reproduced by Chinese embassy

rows.source: Indonesia budget growth: nominal versus real and endpoint
rows.usage: The passage says Indonesia’s defense budget nearly quadrupled over the preceding decade, citing 2009 and 2020 figures in note 130.
rows.finding: The note’s 33.7-to-127.4 trillion rupiah figures imply 3.78 times the starting nominal amount, or about 278 percent growth. That arithmetic supports nearly quadrupled on those endpoints. The official Australian 2020 review reports 108.4 trillion for 2019, rather than the note’s 109.6, and shows real declines in 2018–2019. Reconcile original, revised and proposed budgets; label the growth nominal and avoid describing every year as growing steadily. Consistency review, November 14, 2026. Label the 3.78 multiplier as the ratio of the quoted nominal rupiah endpoints. CMS17-R11 distinguishes the original ministry budget and the revised request. The Australian series has a different 2019 value and records intervening real declines. The growth claim needs those qualifications before applying to a real series.
evidence: Australian Defence Economic Trends 2020, Indonesia pp. 12–13

rows.source: Indonesia white paper: 274-vessel minimum force
rows.usage: Note 141 attributes a 274-vessel minimum force divided into strike, patrol and support groups to the 2008 Indonesian defense white paper.
rows.finding: The indexed Indonesian Ministry of Defence copy explicitly states 274 ships of various types and lists the three corresponding force groups. Its support-force list also includes multipurpose transports, tankers, ocean tugs and hydro-oceanographic ships. This resolves the suggestion that the number was absent from the white paper. The Indonesian pagination is p. 127; verify the English edition separately for the cited p. 110.
evidence: Official Indonesian 2008 white paper, indexed p. 127

rows.source: Panther purchase: announcement, signature and local work
rows.usage: The note is attached to: “The purchase of a total of eleven of the Panthers was announced in April 2014, with the helicopters manufactured jointly, by the Indonesian aerospace firm PT Dirgantara (PTDI) in cooperation with Airbus Helicopters.”
rows.finding:
**Open-claim evidence follow-up, November 22, 2026 — Reviewed; unresolved.** The supplied passage gives eleven Panthers, an April 2014 announcement and joint manufacture. The manufacturer’s previously located delivery release distinguishes a late-2014 signed contract and PTDI reassembly/mission-equipment work, but the active URL now returns 404. Announcement, contract signature, delivery and local completion are different milestones. The April date and the breadth of joint-manufacture wording remain unverified.

**Remaining gap or scope limit.** An accessible contemporary April announcement and manufacturer record specifying the local industrial role.

**Earlier audit record (preserved).** Airbus’s release confirms eleven helicopters, a contract signed in late 2014, and a role for PT Dirgantara Indonesia in reassembly and mission-equipment installation. It does not establish an April 2014 purchase announcement. Preserve the confirmed count and industrial roles, but obtain a contemporaneous announcement for April or state the supported late-2014 contract milestone. Announcement and signing need not share a date.
evidence: Original Airbus delivery and contract account

rows.usage: Note 236 describes China’s occupation of Mischief Reef as occurring the previous April, citing Dupont p. 60.
rows.finding:
**Open-claim evidence follow-up, November 22, 2026 — Reviewed; unresolved.** The supplied paragraph connects Suharto’s June 1995 approval with a former attaché’s reference to the previous April. The cited Dupont p. 60, rather than the grouped note’s other p. 54 locator, is needed to determine what the quotation refers to. JSTOR returned a challenge page, not the article. A general Mischief Reef timeline cannot identify a quotation’s specific referent.

**Remaining gap or scope limit.** The actual Dupont p. 60 passage and distinction between occupation, discovery, announcement and later reaction.

**Earlier audit record (preserved).** The Dupont article’s identity was located on JSTOR, but p. 60 was not available in the retrieved text. The passage’s reference to the previous April must be checked in the original context: occupation, discovery, public disclosure and Indonesian reaction could refer to different events. Do not assign a corrected month from a general chronology without establishing which event Dupont and the cited speaker meant. Consistency review, November 14, 2026. The same discipline used in CMR07-R18 applies here. A contemporaneous announcement, public disclosure and the underlying event can have different dates. No available text of Dupont p. 60 establishes which date the speaker intended. Follow-up review, November 14, 2026. The originating grouped note identifies p. 54 while the specific event quotation points to p. 60. That distinction matters. An incident timeline elsewhere cannot supply the referent of previous April in the second passage.

rows.source: King Air inventory: four aircraft and the cited AMTI page
rows.usage: The passage attributes four Beechcraft 200T aircraft in the RMAF inventory to Vuving’s 2017 AMTI account.
rows.finding:
**Open-claim evidence follow-up, November 22, 2026 — Reviewed; unresolved.** Read the cited AMTI account’s air-force narrative and inventory discussion. It lists several transport categories but does not identify Beechcraft 200T or King Air. It therefore does not substantiate the four-aircraft statement as cited. paper_memo.memo_title: Analytical & Source-Audit Memo: CMS-17 — The Maritime Fulcrum of the Indo-Pacific (Scott Bentley, CMSI, 2023)

sections.heading: 1. Strategic Context & Core Thesis
sections.body: China Maritime Study No. 17 shifts the focus of South China Sea analysis from the Spratlys and Paracels to the **southernmost reaches of the nine-dash line**, where China's coast guard and maritime militia have pushed toward Indonesia's Natuna Islands and Malaysia's South Luconia Shoals since 2010. Scott Bentley argues that China's operational successes in the north (Scarborough, the Spratly outposts) have not translated into control in the south because **Indonesia and Malaysia are capable and determined**: they arrest and expel Chinese fishing vessels, build larger coast guard ships and bases, and align quietly with the United States and Australia. Because Chinese control requires rival claimants to acquiesce, the political decisions in Jakarta and Kuala Lumpur are the fulcrum of the contest. The monograph is organized around the 2016 incidents, a country chapter on each state and a policy conclusion for Washington.

sections.heading: 2. Section-by-Section Analytical Breakdown
sections.body:
• **Introduction (pp. 1–6)**: The March–June 2016 incidents and the 'fulcrum' thesis.
• **China's Creeping Southward Expansion (pp. 6–12)**: Claims and firsts since 2016, Scarborough as the northern template, Vietnam's blocks and the 'fragile control' argument.
• **Running into Regional Powers (pp. 12–13)**: ASEAN, hedging and the defense-cooperation context.
• **Indonesia (pp. 13–58)**: Historic perceptions of China, the incidents since 2010, base upgrades, navy and coast guard modernization (Table 1), and ties with the United States and Australia.
• **Malaysia (pp. 58–85)**: Mahathir-era and later policies, South Luconia, navy and MMEA modernization (Table 2), and the 'low-key alignment with the West.'
• **Conclusion (pp. 88–93)**: The fulcrum, expertise gaps in the US and partner preferences.

sections.heading: 3. Key Doctrinal Concepts, Terminology & Quantitative Claims
sections.body:
• **Concepts**: *maritime fulcrum*, *creeping expansion*, *control* as acquiescence by rival claimants, *echelon defense* (after Martinson), *historic rights*, *traditional fishing grounds*, *capabilities-based planning*, *Global Maritime Fulcrum* (Jokowi), *nonalignment with a Western tilt*.
• **Quantitative claims**: CCG 3304 rammed on `20 March 2016`; `>100` Chinese fishing vessels expelled `15 nm` from the Indonesia–Malaysia boundary (`24 March`); `>50` ships in the Dec 2019–Jan 2020 fishing fleet; `>700 nm` from Hainan, `<100 nm` from Natuna Besar; BAKAMLA `10` ships, `$56 million`, `2,000` personnel (`5×`); DKP `~35` ships, `$16 million`, `<1,000` personnel; MMEA `~130` → `228` vessels, `5,369` → `9,400` personnel, `8` → `27` aircraft; Indonesia's Jan 2020 deployment of `>12` ships.

sections.heading: 4. Audit Assessment & Analytical Significance
sections.body:
Of the 6 reference rows audited in `CMS-17`, 5 are rated `ok` (one with table slips) and 1 is rated `unk`; no substantive `fix` was found:
• **`[CMS17-R01]` (`ok` — 2016 Incidents)**: The sequence matches `CMS-15` and press reports; Bentley's 'three months' is more exact than Martinson's 'four.'
• **`[CMS17-R04]` (`ok · slip` — MMEA Table 2)**: The planned growth ratios are consistent, but the table lists a '157 mm' gun for a 1,300-ton ship and omits the Bagan Datuk class named in the text.
• **`[CMS17-R05]` (`unk` — China's 'Firsts')**: The 'first time' claims about overlapping claims and historic rights are not reconcilable with earlier Chinese legal texts and CMS-15.

This is the **fullest English-language study of Indonesia's and Malaysia's responses to China at sea**: the incident chronologies, force-structure counts and budgets are drawn from regional press and agency sources and are internally consistent. Its framing argument — that Chinese control hinges on political acquiescence in Jakarta and Kuala Lumpur — is a judgment rather than a finding, and its optimism about alignment with the United States is the part most exposed to the political changes after March 2020.

**Footnote rows**: all 474 footnotes were extracted and consolidated into 325 source rows in the Reference Audit Matrix (CMS17-N001 to CMS17-N475). Repeat citations of the same source within this paper, including Ibid. and short-form notes, share one row, which lists each note's passage and result. Footnote-level result: 474 notes: 182 (38%) are confirmed, 6 of them against a retrieved source and 176 after an outside web search (129 of the latter with a slip or an unchecked detail noted); 30 are flagged for reader check; 292 (62%) are not confirmed. Of the 292 notes not confirmed, 42 were judged not web-checkable (1 the authors' own data, imagery or analysis; 2 private interviews or conversations; 20 print-only books or paywalled items; 1 note that is explanatory text or a fragment, not a citation; 18 other items); 250 were searched on the web without finding corroboration. A source row is `ok` only when every note in it is confirmed, and `fix` when a note is confirmed wrong; the paper's 325 source rows are 121 `ok`, 0 `fix` and 204 `unk`. Notes flagged for reader check, for example (the outside search found something a reader should look at; none is a finding that the author is wrong): `CMS17-N007`: The sentence says a large Chinese fishing fleet of over fifty ships operated in the southern South China Sea from December 2019 to January 2020, escorted by multiple CCG patrol ships; `CMS17-N011`: The sentence says that in January 2020 Indonesia conducted its largest-ever operational deployment of navy and coast guard ships to the South China Sea, sending over a dozen surface combatants and patrol ships; `CMS17-N016`: The sentence says that in March 2016, following the CCG ramming incident, China declared for the first time that the location of a specific incident fell within its "traditional fishing grounds." The March 2016 statement (Hua Chunying, 21 March) is confirmed; and 27 more. 93 notes carry a reader note on how the note is displayed or cited.

paper_memo.memo_title: Analytical & Source-Audit Memo: CMS-18 — Sea Dragons: Special Operations and Chinese Military Strategy (John Chen & Joel Wuthnow, CMSI, 2025)

sections.heading: 1. Strategic Context & Core Thesis
sections.body: China Maritime Study No. 18 is the first systematic English-language study of the **PLA Navy Marine Corps' special operations brigade**, the 'Sea Dragons' (formally the PLANMC 7th Brigade, Unit 91128). John Chen and Joel Wuthnow argue that the unit, though small — about 3,000 people, just over 1% of the navy — has become a key enabler of China's maritime strategy across three layers: wartime support to island-landing and blockade campaigns (above all against Taiwan), coercion of rivals through more provocative exercises, and non-war missions such as antipiracy and noncombatant evacuations. They identify five limits (end strength, weak integration with joint commands, training quality, thin real-world experience and equipment) and offer observable signposts of progress. The analysis rests on Chinese doctrinal texts, People's Navy and PLA media, trade publications and footage rather than any official unit disclosure.

sections.heading: 2. Section-by-Section Analytical Breakdown
sections.body:
• **Introduction (pp. 1–3)**: *Operation Red Sea*, the questions and the sources.
• **Strategy and Doctrine (pp. 3–9)**: PLA concepts of SOF, historical and foreign analogies, self-critique, and maritime SOF missions in amphibious warfare and beyond.
• **The Sea Dragons: An Organizational Portrait (pp. 9–16)**: Basing, structure, leaders, personnel and equipment (Tables 1–2, Figures 2–7).
• **Training (pp. 16–24)**: Individual, unit, combined-arms, joint and foreign training.
• **Operational Experience (pp. 24–25)**: Antipiracy, Yemen, Sudan and Djibouti.
• **Supporting and Assisting Units (pp. 25–28)**: Marine reconnaissance battalions, aviation, salvage and rescue, minesweepers and bases.
• **Contributions and Challenges (pp. 28–35)**: Cross-strait and coercive roles, constraints and signposts.

sections.heading: 3. Key Doctrinal Concepts, Terminology & Quantitative Claims
sections.body:
• **Concepts**: *special combat force* (特种作战力量), *system destruction warfare*, *multi-domain integrated joint operations*, *quadphibious*, *fendui*, *brigade-battalion-company*, *noncombatant evacuation*, *nonwar military operations*, *joint special operations group*, *SOCOM-like functional command*.
• **Quantitative claims**: `~3,000` personnel (`1.15%` of `260,000`); `12` companies in `4` battalions; `7` fendui; `12` officers in Table 1; `15` army SOF brigades vs. `1` navy and `1` air force; `>50%` attrition; `<=1/3` transferred in; `~70` SOF on the 2008 task force; `~50` Sea Dragons and `571` people in the Yemen evacuation; `$500+ million` for *Operation Red Sea*; SOF ratios `1:122`, `1:30`, `1:25`.

sections.heading: 4. Audit Assessment & Analytical Significance
sections.body:
Of the 6 reference rows audited in `CMS-18`, 4 are rated `ok` (two with figure or total slips) and 2 are rated `unk`; no substantive `fix` was found:
• **`[CMS18-R02]` (`ok · slip` — Figures 4–5 vs. Text)**: The text's 'eleven squadrons' does not match Figure 4's twelve, and Figure 5 labels company-level units 'squadrons.'
• **`[CMS18-R04]` (`ok · slip` — Yemen Evacuation Total)**: '571' is the Chinese-national subtotal; the Foreign Ministry's full total was higher.
• **`[CMS18-R03]` (`unk` — 3,000 End Strength)**: The arithmetic checks, but the headline number rests on unnamed sources.
• **`[CMS18-R05]` (`unk` — Doctrinal Quotations)**: The Chinese-language doctrinal quotations could not be retrieved.

The study is the **best open-source baseline on a deliberately opaque unit** and is careful to separate confirmed from assessed organization (the figure keys do this). Its main limits are the ones it states: the picture comes from Chinese media and doctrine, not from any authoritative organization chart, and most quantitative claims about the brigade — size, selection rate, share of transferees — are therefore estimates.

**Footnote rows**: all 196 footnotes were extracted and consolidated into 124 source rows in the Reference Audit Matrix (CMS18-N001 to CMS18-N197). Repeat citations of the same source within this paper, including Ibid. and short-form notes, share one row, which lists each note's passage and result. Footnote-level result: 196 notes: 24 (12%) are confirmed, 1 of them against a retrieved source and 23 after an outside web search (22 of the latter with a slip or an unchecked detail noted); 1 is flagged for reader check; 172 (88%) are not confirmed. Of the 172 notes not confirmed, 121 are Chinese-language sources that have not been searched in Chinese (a search in Chinese could settle some of them); 8 were judged not web-checkable (2 the authors' own data, imagery or analysis; 6 other items); 43 were searched on the web without finding corroboration. A source row is `ok` only when every note in it is confirmed, and `fix` when a note is confirmed wrong; the paper's 124 source rows are 13 `ok`, 0 `fix` and 111 `unk`. Notes flagged for reader check, for example (the outside search found something a reader should look at; none is a finding that the author is wrong): `CMS18-N133`: The sentence says Sea Dragons members, including two future company commanders, trained at Venezuelan military special forces schools. The searches found only reports in the other direction: StrategyPage (2006) and Diálogo describe PLA (army) special forces instructors training Venezuelan commandos, and nothing links the PLA…. 28 notes carry a reader note on how the note is displayed or cited.
